extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students of moral philosophy / Christian ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository moral-philosophical guidance on Stoic and Christian conceptions of virtue and practical instruction for cultivating 'humanity' (love of mankind), including prescriptive methods (precept, removal of hindrances, example) and critiques of rival systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as the sole real good / act irrespective of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoic doctrine that 'there is no real good but virtue' and that a good man should act irrespectively of reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with emphasis that virtue must be pursued for its own sake, not for posthumous fame or material reward; contrasted with Epicurean willingness to sublimate pleasure as an end. Quotations: 'He who wishes his virtue to be blazed abroad is not labouring for virtue but for fame.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not seek ostentation; virtue for conscience not praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions are most laudable when done 'without ostentation, and far from the sight of men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated Stoic injunctions: 'Nothing for opinion, all for conscience.' and 'That which is beautiful is beautiful in itself; the praise of man adds nothing to its quality.' Advice: cultivate duties done for their intrinsic worth rather than visibility or acclaim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason and will must predominate; suppression of the affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoical ideal: complete suppression of the affections to make way for the absolute ascendency of reason; the will-directed character is morally superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two educational types correspond: (a) strengthen the will (Spartan/stoical systems, asceticism) to endure pain and repress desires; (b) guide desires to make virtue attractive. Warning: excessive suppression mutilates humanity and reduces benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clemency (judgment) distinguished from pity (vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seneca's detailed distinction: clemency is an habitual disposition to gentleness in punishment (an act of judgment), whereas pity is a weakness that disturbs judgment and contemplates only suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Clemency adjudicates upon the proportion between suffering and guilt. Pity contemplates only suffering, and gives no thoughts to its cause.' Anti-pattern: praising tearful sympathy as superior to reasoned mercy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education models: strengthen the will vs. guide the desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct theories of education: one aims chiefly to strengthen the will (suited to disturbed/military societies), the other to make virtue attractive and draw desires to virtuous ends (suited to organised, tranquil civilisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: choose pedagogical methods according to social context; heroic self-denial systems produce rare heroic virtue but are ill-suited for most people; making virtue attractive better influences ordinary characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraternity and universal benevolence as Stoic precept
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoics taught the fraternity of all men and the duty of consecrating life to the welfare of others, extending compassion 'even to crime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They developed detailed precepts of philanthropy, treated guilt as ignorance, and declared prevention the only legitimate ground of punishment. Guidance: enact wide-ranging, reasoned, passionless philanthropy rather than narrow emotional charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique: stoicism's impracticality for common life
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism's high standard of self-control makes it unfit for the majority of mankind and ordinary affairs; moral systems must accommodate common characters and mingled motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A social moral system should tincture, modify, and mitigate where it cannot eradicate; otherwise it will be rejected by the multitude. Practical rule: design moral prescriptions with attention to typical human temperament and daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine that 'all virtues are equal' and related paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic claims that all virtues (and all vices) are the same, and that nothing is an evil which does not affect the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a speculative consequence that produces unnatural and affected appearances; warning that flattening gradations of moral value undermines moral realism and practical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity of man and exaltation of pride as moral motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic elevation of dignity and pride (an inward self-approbation) as a central moral agent distinct from vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sense of virtue occupies in stoicism a role analogous to the sense of sin in Christianity; critique notes the absence of repentance and the failure to appreciate moral purification through contrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of suicide as refuge and attitude to death
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism culminated in the doctrine that suicide can be a legitimate refuge against extreme suffering or despair; death is often regarded as a remedy rather than a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a logical outcome of the system's self-reliance and denial of humiliation; critique: this perspective reflects limits in stoic conception of human good and suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct training method: make humanity a duty to feel ('Love your neighbour')
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ's first method is direct: command people to feel the passion—'Love one's neighbour as oneself' and 'Love your enemies'—making the passion a point of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that the command isn't to create feeling by will, but to remove hindrances so natural love can arise. Practical advice: use authoritative precept to restore natural benevolence where corrupted by social maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove social causes that paralyse the heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold, distrustful societies produce habits of self-defence that stifle natural affections; individuals must be told to shake off distrust, unproved suspicions, and causeless jealousies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction: identify and remove removable causes (habitual suspicion, cynical maxims) that impede the natural emergence of sympathy; an exhortation to deliberate effort to revive warmth of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precept plus practice: minority-by-example strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: A small minority abandoning selfish maxims and behaving as if others were friends can shame and convert others; 'let that minority for itself abandon the selfish theory ... by sincerity and persistency it will gradually convert the majority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactic: minority groups should openly renounce retaliation and self-defence, act benevolently, and thereby induce broader social change by example rather than mere proclamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disarmament principle: be harmless and accept suffering as discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ commands followers to 'disarm at once'—be 'as sheep in the midst of wolves' and 'harmless as doves'; injuries may be expected but not retaliated against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: patience and non-retaliation wean followers from self and may shame exploiters; the discipline of suffering can expand channels of humanity within individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity is learned from exposure to noble examples; belief in one model can revive compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity is not a blind instinct but a love for the race founded on experience of noble qualities in particular people; strength of humanity is proportional to acquaintance with admirable examples, and 'the most lost cynic will get a new heart by learning thoroughly to believe in the virtue of one man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for moral formation: cultivate, publicise, and remember exemplary lives and deeds; even one authentic exemplar can regenerate humane feeling in a pessimist.
